extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic/philosophy; anyone learning the theory of propositions and classification of names
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and classificatory criteria for analyzing the form, varieties, and import of propositions (affirmative/negative, simple/compound, modal, universal/particular, hypothetical, etc.), and for classifying what can be named (feelings, minds, bodies, attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of all Namable Things
rubrics_metrics.description: An enumeration and classification of all Namable Things into four classes: (1) Feelings or States of Consciousness; (2) Minds which experience those feelings; (3) Bodies, or external objects which excite certain of those feelings, together with the powers or properties whereby they excite them; (4) The Successions and Co-existences, the Likenesses and Unlikenesses, between feelings or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four classes (feelings, minds, bodies, relations among feelings) are proposed as a substitute for Aristotle's categories. Practical application will appear in inquiry into the Import of Propositions. Distinguish Psychological/Subjective facts (composed solely of feelings) from Objective facts (composed wholly or in part of substances and attributes); every objective fact is grounded on a corresponding subjective one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copula as sign of predication (avoid ambiguity with existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The copula (typically forms of 'to be') is primarily a sign of predication — a linguistic device indicating that a predicate is affirmed or denied of a subject — and should not be confused with a signifier of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure no indistinctness in conception of the copula: e.g., 'A centaur is a fiction of the poets' uses 'is' without asserting existence. Confusing the copula's role with existence has produced many metaphysical errors; detect ambiguities by comparing usage across languages. The same word ('is') can serve as copula or as existential predicate; maintain the distinction in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Affirmative and Negative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions divide into affirmative (predicate affirmed of the subject) and negative (predicate denied of the subject). The copula 'is' signals affirmation; 'is not' signals negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of treatments (e.g., Hobbes) that treat negation as mere affirmation of a negative name ('not-dead') — this verbal maneuver obscures the real distinction between asserting a fact and asserting its non-existence. Recognize that denying is asserting absence, not presence; maintain the factual distinction between 'Cæsar is dead' and 'Cæsar is not dead.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality and tense properly attach to the copula
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of tense (past, present, future) and modal qualifications (may, perhaps, possible) are aspects of the predication as a whole and properly considered as attaching to the copula rather than the predicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat temporal and modal qualifications as modifying the act of predication (the copula), not the predicate itself. Note that modal expressions that express the speaker's state of mind (e.g., 'Cæsar may be dead' meaning 'I am not sure he is alive') relate to our epistemic state; distinguish these from objective modality of the proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple (categorical) vs Compound (complex) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple proposition affirms or denies one predicate of one subject. A compound (or complex) proposition contains more than one predicate or subject (or both) and often consists of several propositions connected by conjunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many so-called complex propositions are really multiple propositions joined (e.g., 'Cæsar is dead and Brutus is alive' = two propositions). Conjunctions and particles are abbreviations of further propositions. When combined by 'or' or 'if', the resulting forms (disjunctive, conditional) may express a single assertion (inferential relation) rather than a mere aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical/Conditional vs Categorical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical (conditional) propositions assert an inferential relation between propositions (e.g., 'If A then B'); categorical propositions assert directly about subjects and predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In conditionals the subject and predicate are themselves propositions (the proposition 'B is an inference from A'). Understand that disjunctive propositions can be rendered as conditionals; a hypothetical's import is about inferability, not an affirmation of either component proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal, Particular, Indefinite, and Singular propositions (quantity of predication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification based on the degree of generality of the subject: Universal (predicate affirmed/denied of all members: 'All men are mortal'), Particular (of some members: 'Some men are mortal'), Indefinite (form unclear whether universal or particular), Singular (subject is an individual: 'Julius Caesar is mortal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to detect intended quantity; context or usage often supplies whether an expression like 'Man is mortal' is universal. Recognize that 'indefinite' often reflects a failure to mark intended quantity, but the speaker intends either universal or particular. 'Most', 'some', etc., are treated as particular when portion is left unspecified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A term is distributed when it stands for each and every individual denoted by it. In universal propositions the subject is distributed; in particular propositions the subject is undistributed. Distribution of predicate varies by form (e.g., 'No men have wings' distributes both subject and predicate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply distribution to analyze syllogisms: a universal proposition = distributed subject; a particular proposition = undistributed subject. Use distribution to assess inferential validity and to express syllogistic rules concisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions concern things, not merely ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing the import of a proposition, focus on the fact or thing asserted (the external phenomena) rather than on the mental act of judging or on relations between ideas. Propositions are about external facts even though mental ideas are involved in believing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject theories that reduce propositions to relations between ideas alone. Distinguish between the psychological event of having ideas and the objective fact the proposition asserts (e.g., 'fire causes heat' concerns natural phenomena, not my ideas of fire and heat). This distinction affects the analysis of what propositions mean and what truth consists in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that propositions can be subjects/predicates (meta-propositional predication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions themselves may be predicated of: e.g., 'That the whole is greater than its part is an axiom in mathematics' — here the subject is an entire proposition and predicates are affirmed of propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering such uses, treat them as assertions about propositions (their status, inferability, acceptance) rather than confusing them with ordinary subject-predicate assertions about objects. This allows logical analysis of assertions about doctrines, inferences, tenets, axioms, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbal simplifications that obscure substantive distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplifying logical distinctions by rephrasing (e.g., treating negation as affirmation of a negative name, or reducing tense/modality to predicate modification) is often merely verbal and can obscure real, factual distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer analyses that respect the factual differences (e.g., between a fact and its non-existence, between different tenses/modalities) rather than collapsing them into uniform verbal forms. Be alert to cases where apparent simplification increases conceptual confusion rather than clarifying it.
